units.title: Unit 33 — Personal finance
learningObjectives: Use natural collocations to discuss income, expenditure, borrowing and debt repayment.
Distinguish overdraft arrangements, credit limits, outstanding debts and complete repayment.
Recognise financial-crime expressions and describe the effects of missed payments.
Choose accurate banking verb–noun combinations and explain register differences.

items.example: The independent bookshop managed to stay afloat despite a difficult winter.
items.note: A financial metaphor for continuing to meet expenses rather than becoming insolvent.

items.example: Freelance translation became her main source of income after graduation.
items.note: A source of income is where regular or occasional earnings come from.

items.example: Evening classes can help experienced teachers supplement their income.
items.note: Supplement means add to existing earnings; it does not mean replace all income.

items.example: He took out a student loan to cover the final year of tuition.
items.note: A loan is borrowed money that normally has to be repaid.

items.example: Even a few hours of part-time work helped her cover transport costs.
items.note: Part-time work means employment with fewer working hours than a comparable full-time position.

items.example: Before starting her new job, Sofia decided to open a current account.
items.note: In British English, a current account is used for everyday banking transactions.

items.example: It is easy to get into debt when household bills rise unexpectedly.
items.note: Get into debt describes entering the state of owing money.

items.example: His priority this year is to clear his debts before moving house.
items.note: Clear debts means pay them off completely, not merely reduce the balance.

items.example: We agreed to cut down on luxuries while saving for the deposit.
items.note: Cut down on something means consume or spend less of it, not necessarily stop entirely.

items.example: A series of expensive purchases caused the company to run up huge debts.
items.note: Run up debts highlights gradual accumulation through spending or borrowing.

items.example: You can make a payment through the banking app before the due date.
items.note: The natural verb with payment is make; a payment may be partial or full.

items.example: Credit-card debt grew quickly because the unpaid balance attracted interest.
items.note: The noun credit-card describes the origin of the debt, not a separate loan product.

items.example: Her agreed credit limit was lower than the amount she wanted to spend.
items.note: A credit limit is the maximum borrowing allowance authorised by the provider.

items.example: The bank sent an alert before she could exceed her credit limit.
items.note: Exceed means go beyond a specified amount; do not use surpass in this banking formula.

items.example: The firm had to borrow heavily to finance an ambitious expansion.
items.note: Borrow heavily emphasises a large amount of borrowing rather than physical weight.

items.example: The accountant listed every outstanding debt before preparing the budget.
items.note: Outstanding means still unpaid; it does not mean excellent in this financial context.

items.example: She aims to pay back a loan within three years.
items.note: Pay back a loan describes returning the money that was borrowed.

items.example: Several emergency repairs made him run up an overdraft.
items.note: An overdraft occurs when an eligible bank account has a negative balance.

items.example: The student account offered an interest-free overdraft for a limited period.
items.note: Interest-free means no interest is charged under the stated terms and limits.

items.example: The bank blocked suspicious transactions after detecting credit-card fraud.
items.note: Credit-card fraud involves unauthorised or deceptive use of a payment card.

items.example: Identity theft can occur when criminals obtain personal details from a fake website.
items.note: Identity theft means taking identifying information to impersonate someone.

items.example: Reports of suspicious transfers reached an all-time high last quarter.
items.note: An all-time high is the highest recorded level, not merely a recent increase.

items.example: The restaurant spent a fortune renovating its original kitchen.
items.note: Spend a fortune is informal and means spend a very large amount.

items.example: During the conference, the visitors ran up a bill at the hotel café.
items.note: Run up a bill means accumulate charges before settling them.

items.example: The audit found that a senior employee had tried to falsify records.
items.note: Falsify records means deliberately alter records to mislead, not simply make an error.

items.example: The insurer rejected several fraudulent claims submitted with altered receipts.
items.note: Fraudulent claims are knowingly dishonest requests for money or benefits.

items.example: We decided to put down a deposit to reserve the small apartment.
items.note: Put down a deposit means pay part of a total price in advance.

items.example: Low interest rates made the mortgage more attractive to first-time buyers.
items.note: Interest rates describe the price of borrowing, expressed as a rate.

items.example: If a borrower defaults on repayments, the lender may take legal action.
items.note: Default on repayments means fail to pay as required, rather than merely pay late once.

items.pt: exigir a quitação de um empréstimo
items.example: After repeated breaches of the contract, the lender chose to call in a loan.
items.note: Call in a loan means demand repayment, often earlier than originally expected.

items.example: The lender agreed to write off debts that could no longer be recovered.
items.note: Write off debts means recognise that amounts will not be collected.

items.example: Management introduced cost-cutting measures without cancelling staff training.
items.note: The standard combination is measures, not cost-cutting methods in this sense.

items.pt: contratar um limite de cheque especial
items.example: Before the contract payment arrived, he asked the bank to arrange an overdraft.
items.note: Arrange an overdraft means agree access to a temporary negative balance.

items.example: After the client disappeared, the accountant classified the invoice as a bad debt.
items.note: In accounting, a bad debt is unlikely to be recovered.

items.example: Years of unpaid bills left the business deep in debt.
items.note: Deep in debt intensifies the seriousness of an indebted position.

items.example: The minister outlined a plan to reduce the national debt over time.
items.note: The national debt refers to outstanding borrowing accumulated by the national government.

items.example: It took her six months to pay off a debt from an unexpected medical bill.
items.note: Pay off emphasises clearing a debt in full.

items.example: Investors were cautious about the debt-ridden retailer.
items.note: Debt-ridden describes a person, firm or institution burdened by debt.

items.example: Unexpected repair costs left the household with a hefty overdraft.
items.note: Hefty suggests an unusually large amount in an informal tone.

items.example: The new account included an overdraft facility for temporary shortfalls.
items.note: A facility is an agreed banking arrangement, not the negative balance itself.

items.example: The bank applied fees after the account entered an unauthorised overdraft.
items.note: Unauthorised indicates borrowing beyond an agreed limit or without approval.

items.example: The compliance officer asked for evidence of the source of funds.
items.note: Source of funds identifies where the money came from; it differs from income.

units.title: Unit 34 — The economy
learningObjectives: Discuss inflation, interest rates, economic growth and industrial performance accurately.
Use public-policy collocations for taxation, social opportunity and the allocation of resources.
Contrast increasing and falling economic indicators without confusing the agents of change.
Recognise formal language characteristic of budget speeches and economic reports.

items.example: The central bank announced new measures to curb inflation.
items.note: Curb inflation means restrain its rise, not necessarily push prices back to earlier levels.

items.example: Rampant inflation had already eroded purchasing power before the reforms began.
items.note: Rampant conveys rapid, uncontrolled growth and strong negative evaluation.

items.example: The current economic climate has made firms cautious about hiring.
items.note: Economic climate refers to prevailing conditions, not the weather.

items.example: Higher interest rates can increase monthly loan repayments.
items.note: Interest rates are conventionally raised, lowered or kept unchanged.

items.example: The monetary committee voted to raise interest rates by a quarter point.
items.note: Raise is transitive: an institution raises rates; rates rise on their own.

items.example: Diversified funds may appeal to people who want to invest for the long term.
items.note: Long-term investment considers a longer horizon, not immediate returns.

items.example: Policymakers tried to steer the economy away from a severe recession.
items.note: Steer suggests guiding economic developments, often through policy choices.

items.example: The region experienced uninterrupted economic growth for five consecutive years.
items.note: Uninterrupted means growth continued without a break throughout the stated period.

items.example: Targeted investment in infrastructure may stimulate growth.
items.note: Stimulate growth means encourage expansion; stunt growth means restrict it.

items.example: The agency reported that production expanded at an annual rate of three percent.
items.note: Annual rate expresses a pace over a year, often annualised from shorter data.

items.example: The cooperative reported steady growth rather than sharp quarterly swings.
items.note: Steady growth is gradual and consistent, not necessarily rapid.

items.section: Budget speech · Industry and public policy
items.example: A thriving industry can create demand for technical specialists.
items.note: Thriving means doing particularly well; it is stronger than merely operating.

items.section: Budget speech · Industry and public policy
items.example: Automation allowed the factory to increase output without adding a second shift.
items.note: Output is the quantity of goods or services produced.

items.section: Budget speech · Industry and public policy
items.example: The association negotiated new rules to safeguard the interests of small suppliers.
items.note: Safeguard interests means protect the position or welfare of a group.

items.section: Budget speech · Industry and public policy
items.example: Management blamed plummeting profits on higher transport costs.
items.note: Plummeting means falling very rapidly; it contrasts with soaring.

items.section: Budget speech · Industry and public policy
items.example: Reliable public services are essential in isolated communities.
items.note: Public services are typically funded or organised for general social use.

items.section: Budget speech · Industry and public policy
items.example: The council assessed whether the new system offered value for money.
items.note: Value for money means benefits or quality justify the amount spent.

items.section: Budget speech · Industry and public policy
items.example: The proposal would redirect public spending towards basic healthcare.
items.note: Public spending is expenditure by the state, not private household spending.

items.section: Budget speech · Industry and public policy
items.example: The scholarship initiative aims to extend opportunity to rural students.
items.note: Extend opportunity means make opportunities available to more people.

items.section: Budget speech · Industry and public policy
items.example: Community organisations formed a partnership to tackle social exclusion.
items.note: Tackle an issue means actively work to address it, not claim it is solved.

items.section: Budget speech · Industry and public policy
items.example: Early education can improve life chances for disadvantaged children.
items.note: Life chances refer to future prospects and opportunities in society.

items.section: Budget speech · Industry and public policy
items.example: The government can levy taxes on activities that impose environmental costs.
items.note: Levy taxes usually means impose taxes through legal authority; a levy can name a specific charge.

items.section: Budget speech · Industry and public policy
items.example: The committee agreed to allocate resources to the most urgent repairs.
items.note: Allocate resources means distribute limited money, staff or materials among uses.

items.section: Budget speech · Industry and public policy
items.example: The pilot scheme met with success after a cautious first month.
items.note: Meet with success is a rather formal way to say an attempt was successful.

items.section: Budget speech · Industry and public policy
items.example: The team plans to build on success by extending the programme to new schools.
items.note: Build on success means use previous achievements as a basis for further progress.

items.pt: tributo ambiental relacionado às mudanças climáticas
items.section: Budget speech · Industry and public policy
items.example: The company reviewed how a climate-change levy could affect energy costs.
items.note: Levy names a tax or charge imposed under specific rules; this phrase is policy-specific.

items.section: Budget speech · Industry and public policy
items.example: Unregistered cash transactions can form part of the black economy.
items.note: Black economy denotes undeclared economic activity; the expression has a critical tone.

items.section: Budget speech · Industry and public policy
items.example: Persistent accounting errors may spread if managers leave them unchecked.
items.note: Leave unchecked means fail to restrain or investigate a developing problem.

items.section: Budget speech · Industry and public policy
items.example: Auditors investigated undeclared earnings from informal consulting work.
items.note: Undeclared earnings are income not reported to the relevant tax authority.

items.section: Budget speech · Industry and public policy
items.example: The investigation examined evidence of tax evasion involving hidden accounts.
items.note: Tax evasion means illegal avoidance of taxes and differs from lawful tax planning.

items.section: Budget speech · Industry and public policy
items.example: A shortage of components could push up costs for local manufacturers.
items.note: Push up means cause an increase; the direct object here is costs.

items.section: Budget speech · Industry and public policy
items.example: Rising unemployment prompted the city to expand job-training programmes.
items.note: Rising unemployment means a growing share or number of people out of work.

items.example: Steel production remains an important part of heavy industry in the region.
items.note: Heavy industry typically uses large machinery and substantial raw materials.

items.example: Several traditional industries have been in decline for decades.
items.note: In decline describes a sustained weakening, not just a single bad result.

items.example: Falling unemployment helped improve consumer confidence that year.
items.note: Falling describes the downward trend in unemployment figures.

items.example: A prolonged shortage of credit could stunt growth among small firms.
items.note: Stunt growth means hinder its development; it contrasts with stimulate growth.

items.example: The council decided to introduce a levy on certain commercial deliveries.
items.note: Introduce a levy means establish a new mandatory charge.

items.example: Private spending rose after households regained confidence.
items.note: Private spending contrasts with public spending by government bodies.

items.example: The software company reported soaring profits after launching its new service.
items.note: Soaring conveys a rapid rise and contrasts with plummeting profits.

items.example: Reviewers considered the premium service poor value for money.
items.note: Poor value for money means the return does not justify the price paid.

items.example: Rising costs made the contract less profitable than expected.
items.note: Rising costs focuses on an upward trend, not on one expensive item.
